summary: The paper studies two gate-based quantum finance applications on a simulator: a 2-risk-factor market VaR example and a 2-risk-factor, 2-time-step CCR/PFE example, both using Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation. For market risk, the classical 99% VaR is -5.44 while the q=3 quantum estimate is -6.22 (14% error); for CCR, the classical 90% PFE values are 82 and 134 at t=1 and t=2, versus q=3 estimates of 75 and 127. A third simulator-based noise study shows that 0.1% per-gate noise can induce about 15% error in the 90% CCR quantile and larger noise pushes errors beyond ±25%.

experiments.description: Market risk (VaR) on a two-risk-factor portfolio using quantum amplitude estimation with empirical marginal distributions loaded via piecewise transformations; evaluated on a quantum simulator for q=2 and q=3 qubits per risk factor.

algorithm.variant: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) for VaR/CDF estimation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Two correlated risk-factor return distributions are loaded into separate q-qubit registers; each marginal is first prepared as a normal distribution and then transformed to an empirical distribution via piecewise linear maps. A comparator marks whether normalized P&L is below a threshold for CDF estimation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate VaR from the CDF of normalized portfolio P&L, where ΔP_norm = G1(Z1) + b G2(Z2), and VaR is obtained by bisection search over the CDF.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Integer comparator and thresholding on the P&L register; no QUBO/penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: Two-asset market risk example for a portfolio driven by Microsoft (msft) and Apple (aapl) stock returns over a 10-business-day horizon.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: 10-day overlapping log-returns; zero drift assumption; standardization by sample standard deviation; empirical CDF fit with piecewise cubic and piecewise linear transformations

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Daily closing prices in USD were converted to 10-day overlapping log-returns; mean drift set to zero; returns standardized; empirical marginal CDFs fitted from historical data; Gaussian copula used for dependence; piecewise cubic and piecewise linear fits used for Gk.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Quantum simulator results compared against classical continuous and discretized calculations; IQAE with 1024 shots; VaR reported at 1%, 2.5%, and 5% quantiles.

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical Monte Carlo / classical continuous and discretized reference calculations
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Historical calibration of marginal distributions and Gaussian copula; construction of piecewise transformations; discretization of normal and empirical returns.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Bisection search over the estimated CDF to obtain VaR quantiles; relative error comparison to classical reference.

speedup_claims.conditions: via Quantum Amplitude Estimation; idealized setting
speedup_claims.caveats: Original QAE requires large circuits; practical implementations use improved variants such as IQAE.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) convergence for QAE estimation error

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; only toy-scale q=2 and q=3 per risk factor are reported.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require substantially more qubits than the demonstrated 2- and 3-qubit-per-factor circuits, plus low-noise fault-tolerant execution to preserve QAE benefits.
limiting_factors: Discretization error at q=3 still about 14% for 99% VaR
Classical Monte Carlo and classical continuous reference are already mature
Data loading and circuit depth are substantial

notes: The paper states all computations were carried out on a quantum simulator using Qiskit, but does not name a specific simulator backend; hardware.type inferred as simulator_other.

The paper reports q=2 and q=3 qubits per risk factor, but the total circuit qubit count is not given explicitly; num_qubits left null because the exact total register size is not directly stated in a single value.
The paper reports 99% VaR of -6.22 for q=3 versus classical -5.44, a 14% error, and explicitly states the business case for quantum is not strong.

experiments.description: Counterparty credit risk (PFE) for a two-option portfolio over two future time horizons using quantum amplitude estimation on a quantum simulator; evaluates exposure quantiles at t=1 and t=2 years for q=2 and q=3 qubits per risk factor.

algorithm.variant: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) for exposure CDF/PFE estimation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Two correlated stock-return distributions are loaded for each of two time steps; distributions are added across time; a comparator marks whether exposure is below a threshold for CDF estimation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate PFE quantiles from the CDF of exposure E_t for t=1 and t=2 years, where exposure is derived from the portfolio PV plus collateral and floored at zero in the general setup (the worked example ignores flooring for illustration).
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Comparator-based thresholding for CDF estimation; no QUBO/penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: Two-asset counterparty credit risk example with a portfolio of bought call options on MSFT and AAPL, projected over two years with two equidistant time steps.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: 10-day overlapping log-returns calibrated on four years of historical data; covariance scaled from 10-day to annual horizon; zero drift assumption; Gaussian copula dependence

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Historical 10-day log-returns calibrated from Yahoo! Finance data; covariance matrix scaled by 252/10 for annual horizon; marginal distributions fitted with piecewise cubic/linear transformations; two time steps used for exposure projection.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Quantum simulator results compared to closed-form classical exposure CDFs; IQAE with 1024 shots; exposure quantiles reported at 90%, 95%, and 99% for t=1 and t=2 years.

implementation_details.classical_solver: closed-form classical exposure calculation / classical multivariate normal reference
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Calibration of correlated stock-return distributions; scaling covariance to annual horizon; construction of exposure distributions across time.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: CDF comparison and extraction of 90%, 95%, and 99% PFE quantiles; relative error calculation against classical reference.

speedup_claims.conditions: via Quantum Amplitude Estimation; idealized setting
speedup_claims.caveats: The worked example itself compares against closed-form classical exposure values, not a runtime benchmark.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) convergence for QAE estimation error

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; only q=2 and q=3 per risk factor over two time steps are reported.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require more qubits for better discretization and low-noise hardware; the circuit also needs ancillas for addition and comparison across time steps.
limiting_factors: q=2 gives very large errors; q=3 still only approximate
Multiple time steps increase qubit demand
Classical closed-form benchmark is available and more accurate

notes: The paper states the computations were run on a quantum simulator, but no specific backend/device name is given; hardware.type inferred as simulator_other.
The paper reports q=2 and q=3 qubits per risk factor and notes additional ancillas, but does not provide a single explicit total qubit count for the full circuit; num_qubits left null.
The paper reports q=3 gives 90% PFE values of 75 and 127 versus classical 82 and 134, but does not demonstrate a practical advantage over classical methods.

experiments.description: Noise sensitivity study for the counterparty credit risk circuit, using the same IQAE-based setup as the PFE experiment but with a simplified 0.1% per-gate bit-flip noise model applied to all one- and two-qubit gates and final measurement.

algorithm.variant: IQAE-based PFE estimation under a simplified noise model

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Same exposure-CDF circuit as the CCR experiment, with q=3 qubits per risk factor and t=1 year; noise is injected into all one- and two-qubit gates and the final measurement.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Assess robustness of estimated exposure quantiles/CDF under gate noise.

problem_instance.description: Noise robustness test on the two-asset CCR example at t=1 year.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: Same calibrated distributions as the CCR example; q=3 qubits per risk factor; noise applied post-calibration.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Uses the same calibrated market-risk distributions and exposure circuit as the CCR example; then applies a simplified bit-flip noise model to all one- and two-qubit gates and the final measurement.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare noisy vs noise-free CDFs and quantify relative errors in typical PFE quantiles as noise level varies around 0.1% by powers of two.

noise_model.noise_type: simplified bit-flip noise model; 0.1% per gate on all one- and two-qubit gates and final measurement

implementation_details.classical_solver: noise-free simulator reference / classical CDF comparison
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Reuse of the calibrated CCR model and circuit; construction of a simplified noise model.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Relative error analysis of quantiles versus the noise-free case.

speedup_claims.conditions: same IQAE-based PFE setup under a simplified 0.1% per-gate bit-flip noise model
speedup_claims.caveats: Noise degrades the practical usefulness of the theoretical speedup; the paper reports that even q=3 qubits per risk factor becomes essentially unusable under typical noise levels.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) convergence for QAE estimation error

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not applicable; this is a robustness study rather than a new algorithmic scaling result.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Noise levels would need to be far lower than 0.1% per gate, or error mitigation/fault tolerance would be required.
limiting_factors: 0.1% gate noise already causes about 15% error in the 90% quantile
Errors exceed ±25% at higher noise levels
No advantage over classical baseline is shown

notes: The paper explicitly says the noise study is continued on a quantum simulator, but does not name a specific backend; hardware.type inferred as simulator_noisy.
The paper reports q=3 qubits per risk factor and additional ancillas, but not a single explicit total qubit count; num_qubits left null.

Circuit depth for the noisy variant is not separately reported; the underlying CCR circuit depth is reported elsewhere, but this experiment is specifically the noise-perturbed version, so circuit_depth is left null.
The noise study is explicitly used to show that typical gate noise makes the CCR estimates unusable in practice.

experiments.description: Noise sensitivity study for the counterparty credit risk circuit, using the same IQAE-based setup as the PFE experiment but with a simplified 0.1% per-gate bit-flip noise model applied to all one- and two-qubit gates and final measurement.

algorithm.variant: IQAE-based PFE estimation under a simplified noise model

key_results: At 0.1% noise, the 90% quantile relative error is about 15% for the t=1 CCR case with q=3 qubits per risk factor.
Relative errors exceed ±25% for more pronounced noise levels, rendering the estimates essentially unusable.
